title: s a t
goal: Read and spell the letters s, a, t by sound; blend them into the only real words they can currently make.
newToday: letters s, a, t (sounds /s/, /æ/, /t/) — **one new sound per sitting** (see below), not all three in a single session.
review: yesterday's oral blending games (2 min recap only).
heartLine: a, I (taught in the final combined sitting, once s/a/t are all in).
time: four short sittings — A (~10 min), B (~10 min), C (~15 min), D (~25–30 min). Run one sitting per session (research/01 §5 rule 2: cap new-GPC introduction, mastery-gated, not calendar-gated), or see the fast-track note below.

questions: Which word means someone sat down? ("sat")
Which word starts with the /a/ sound and has just two letters? ("at" or "as")
Think: can you say another word that has only the sounds /s/, /a/, /t/ in some order?

listen.title: Sam's First Day
listen.passage: Sam felt nervous walking into the new classroom. Everyone else already seemed to know each other, chatting and laughing near the window. Sam picked a desk near the back and sat down quietly, hoping nobody would notice how fast their heart was beating. Then a girl named Mia turned around and smiled. "Are you new? I sat exactly where you are on my first day too," she said. "It gets easier by lunchtime, I promise." Sam felt a small knot of worry loosen. Maybe today wouldn't be so bad after all.

tier2.def: feeling worried or a little scared about something that's about to happen.
tier2.full: feeling worried or a little scared about something that's about to happen. "I felt nervous before my first swimming lesson." "She was nervous about the job interview." Your turn: tell me about a time you felt nervous.

tier2.def: to become less tight or less tense.
tier2.full: to become less tight or less tense. "The worried knot in his stomach began to loosen." "Loosen your grip on the rope a little." Your turn: what's something that can loosen?

questions: How did Sam feel at the very start of the story? How do you know?
Why do you think Mia's words helped Sam feel better?

warm.text: none — this is the level's first letter after L1.01's oral-only lesson.

hear.text: /s/ — hissing sound, like a snake. Say "sun...s-s-s-un."

meet.text: "This says /s/." (letter **s**). **Mouth cue:** teeth close together, air hisses out. **Optional multisensory:** trace **s** in the air or in sand while saying /s/.
meet.mouthCue: teeth close together, air hisses out.

mini.text: can the learner produce /s/ instantly, on sight of the letter, 5/5 times? If not, repeat Hear it/Meet it once more before Sitting B.

hear.text: /a/ — short, open mouth, like the start of "apple." Say "at...a-a-at."

meet.text: "This says /a/." (letter **a**). **Mouth cue:** mouth drops open, jaw relaxed.

spell.text: say /a/ → write **a**. Segment and write "sa" (a practice syllable, not scored as a real spelling).

mini.text: s + a, both sounds on sight, 5/5, plus one blend of "sa." If not solid, repeat before Sitting C.

warm.text: flash s, a. Blend "sa" once as a refresher.

hear.text: /t/ — quick tap of the tongue behind the top teeth, like a tiny click. Say "top...t-top."

meet.text: "This says /t/." (letter **t**). **Mouth cue:** tongue taps the ridge behind the top front teeth, then releases.
meet.mouthCue: tongue taps the ridge behind the top front teeth, then releases.

spell.text: say /t/ → write **t**. Segment and write "at," "sat" — these are the first two real, scored spellings of the lesson.

mini.text: all three letter-sounds, 5/5 each; blend all 8 items above at ≥7/8.

sittings.title: s, a, t together: heart words, Read it, Check (~25–30 min)

warm.text: flash s, a, t in mixed order; blend all 8 items from Sitting C once more, faster this time.

heart.note: you already learned this letter says /a/ (like in "at") when it's *inside* a word. On its own, as its own tiny word, it usually says a quick "uh" sound instead (e.g., "a cat"). **Heart part: the "uh" pronunciation** — the letter shape is the one you just learned; only the sound-as-a-standalone-word is the irregular bit to remember.

always a capital letter, always alone as a word, and it says its own letter *name*, "eye." The lowercase letter i (which says /i/ inside words like "pin") isn't formally taught until **L1.03**, tomorrow. For now, treat the whole word **I** as one memorized shape — "heart it": I = "eye," always capital, always by itself.
